statement: A baker places $15$ identical muffins into $4$ different boxes. A box may be left empty, but no box can hold more than $6$ muffins. In how many ways can the muffins be placed?

choices.misconception: I assumed every box must get at least one muffin, so I only counted placements where each box holds between 1 and 6 muffins.
I subtracted the 4 times 165 = 660 placements with an overfull box but did not add back the placements with two overfull boxes.
I subtracted the 165 placements with too many muffins in a box only once, instead of once for each of the 4 boxes.
I used stars and bars, C(18, 3) = 816, and ignored the limit of 6 muffins per box.

hints: Ignore the limit first, then repair the count.
Stars and bars counts every placement. A box that breaks the rule has at least 7 muffins: put 7 in it first and count the rest. Inclusion-exclusion handles two boxes that both break the rule.

All placements: $\binom{18}{3} = 816$. A named box with at least 7: $\binom{11}{3} = 165$. Two named boxes with at least 7 each: 1 muffin left, $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ ways. Three boxes cannot all be overfull.

solutions.reliable: Without the limit, stars and bars gives $\binom{15+3}{3} = 816$ placements. If a particular box has at least 7, put 7 in it and distribute the other 8 freely: $\binom{11}{3} = 165$, and there are 4 choices of box. If two particular boxes each have at least 7, only 1 muffin remains: $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ ways, for each of $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ pairs. Three overfull boxes would need 21 muffins. So the count is $816 - 4 \cdot 165 + 6 \cdot 4 = 816 - 660 + 24 = 180$. Transferable idea: an upper limit becomes a lower limit on the bad cases, which stars and bars can count.
solutions.elegant: Count the empty spaces instead. If box $i$ holds $x_i$ muffins, let $y_i = 6 - x_i$ be its empty spaces. Then $y_1 + y_2 + y_3 + y_4 = 24 - 15 = 9$ with each $y_i \le 6$. Stars and bars with one correction: $\binom{12}{3} - 4\binom{5}{3} = 220 - 40 = 180$ (no two $y_i$ can both be 7 or more).

author: Devansh Sanghavi
